description: We are a passionate team interested in AI, robotics, coding, astronomy, and technology. We enjoy solving problems and building innovative projects. We welcome creative, committed, and curious members with skills in Python, AI, web development, data science, UI/UX, or research. Join us to learn, share ideas, and create something amazing together!
summary:
Our project AgroIntel A.I is a website that provides a support tool that helps farmers explore crop-rotation options using open NASA data. We built an interactive map that combines NASA GIBS MODIS imagery with NASA POWER climate records and real terrain to show field-level risk zones for erosion, drought, flood, frost, nitrogen loss and crop stress. A rotation planner compares three strategies, including the existing rotation, ranked by the farmer’s own priorities such as soil health, water saving and income. Each strategy shows its evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks, and marks which scores come from NASA data and which are agronomic assumptions. Farmers can also type any crop and planting date to see whether it suits their location, and ask an AI agronomist to explain the map or suggest what to plant and when.

This addresses the challenge by turning long-term NASA observations into plain-language guidance on bare-field periods, vulnerable seasons and more resilient rotations. It matters because weather is becoming less predictable and soil health is declining, yet most farmers cannot easily read satellite data. AgroIntel supports, and never replaces, farmer judgment and local expertise.
details:
What AgroIntel does

AgroIntel is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers explore crop-rotation options using open NASA data. A farmer searches for their area, and every part of the site (the map, the AI, the rotation planner, and the crop library) switches to that place.

Main functions

1. Risk heatmap on the map

  • An interactive map shows NASA MODIS imagery (true colour, NDVI, land surface temperature) for any date.
  • A heatmap overlays six risk models: erosion, drought, nitrogen loss, flood, frost, and crop stress.
  • Zones are coloured in five bands, from green (very low) to red (very high), with a legend on the map.
  • Scores combine the NASA POWER daily record for that time of year, each crop’s growth calendar, and real terrain (slope and low spots).
  • Click any zone to see its score and the reason in plain words.
  • A season slider and what-if sliders (rainfall and temperature) show how risk changes.

2. Ask Agro (AI agronomist)

  • Explains the heatmap currently on screen, suggests what to plant and when, and recommends rotations.
  • Can also control the map, e.g., “go to Ohio” or “show frost risk”.

3. Rotation planner

  • Compares three rotation strategies, including the existing one: conventional, legume-integrated, and soil-conservation.
  • The farmer sets six priorities: soil health, water saving, weather resilience, pest and disease break, erosion control, and income.
  • Each strategy shows why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, information gaps, and risks needing local review.
  • Every score is tagged “NASA data” or “Assumption”.

4. Crop library

  • The farmer types any crop and a planting date.
  • The result is Suitable, Suitable with irrigation, Risky, or Not suitable, with temperature, frost, and rainfall reasons and better planting months.
  • About 45 crops are built in; any other crop is answered by the AI and labelled as an AI estimate.

Image of heatmap and AI on the website:

How the AI was developed

We did not train or fine-tune a model. Ask Agro uses Google’s pre-trained Gemini model through our own backend, with a method called grounding: with every question, we send the model the real data for that location and instruct it to answer from that data.

Data given to the AI with each question:

  • NASA-derived climate indicators: temperature anomaly against a 5-year normal, longest dry spell, extreme-rainfall days, and rainfall anomaly.
  • The ranked rotation comparison, with each score tagged as real data or assumption.
  • The heatmap on screen: model, date, each zone’s score,
  • and reason.
  • Monthly climate normals for the place (temperature, rain, frost days, root-zone wetness) from NASA POWER.
  • Planting windows calculated by the site and the recent conversation.

Example code we use for "grounding" the A.I:

{
"question": "Explain the heatmap I'm looking at",
"location_label": "Nakuru, Kenya",
"indicators": { "longest_dry_spell_days": 3, "rainfall_anomaly_pct": -53 },
"page_context": "HEATMAP: Erosion Risk, zones A–E with scores and reasons…"
}

Why this matters: the AI cites real numbers instead of guessing, says clearly what is measured and what is general agronomic knowledge, and admits what it does not know (soil type, local prices, pests).

Benefits and intended impact

  • Turns satellite and climate data into plain-language guidance a farmer can understand.
  • Highlights bare-field periods, vulnerable seasons, and rotations that protect soil and water.
  • Works for any location, with no sensors, hardware, or account, so it is accessible to every farmer across the globe.
  • Intended to support, not replace, farmer judgment and local agricultural expertise.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet.js.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, hosted on Vercel.
  • AI: Google Gemini API.
  • NASA data: NASA GIBS (MODIS Terra/Aqua), NASA POWER.
  • Other data: Open-Meteo elevation (Copernicus DEM), Esri World Imagery, OpenStreetMap Nominatim.
  • Development: GitHub for version control; Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.

What makes it creative

  • The AI sees what the farmer sees: it reads the live map state, so it can explain that exact heatmap.
  • One search drives everything, so the map, AI, planner, and crop check always agree.
  • Real terrain shapes the risk zones: cold air pooling in low spots raises frost risk, and steeper ground raises erosion risk.
  • These tools and website we created is meant to support farmers not replace them.
  • Can be used at any type of device making it easy accessible to farmers across the globe.

What we considered

  • Honesty about data: every score is labelled as measured or assumed by the A.I.
  • Farmer-friendly design: plain words, a glossary of terms (NDVI, evapotranspiration, frost risk) explained on the website so it helps the farmer understand scientific processes in plain language, and light and dark modes that can be toggled by users according to their needs.
  • Limits: crop checks use a short 2023–2026 climate record on a coarse grid of about 50 km; the planner compares three fixed vegetable rotations; the terrain data is not a NASA product. The site states these limits and asks farmers to confirm with local experts.

Where we document our work

    • Website documentation: https://github.com/aizenthegoat123/agrointel-website
    • A.I development documentation: https://github.com/qwfice/agrointel-ai
